claim: Retrosplenial cortex (RSC) plays a key role in incorporating visual information into the brain's spatial framework to represent landmarks.
source: Studies in humans and rodents suggest that retrosplenial cortex (RSC) plays a key role in these computations.
evidence: Supported by citation to existing literature on RSC function in humans and rodents

claim: Head-fixed mice learned the spatial relationship between visual landmark cues and hidden reward locations in an RSC-dependent behavioral task.
source: We developed an RSC-dependent behavioral task in which head-fixed mice learned the spatial relationship between visual landmark cues and hidden reward locations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the behavioral task described in the manuscript

claim: Visual landmark cues served as dominant reference points for most task-active neurons in RSC.
source: Two-photon imaging revealed that these cues served as dominant reference points for most task-active neurons and anchored the spatial code in RSC.
evidence: Supported by two-photon imaging data showing neuronal responses aligned to landmarks

claim: Visual landmark cues anchored the spatial code in RSC.
source: Two-photon imaging revealed that these cues served as dominant reference points for most task-active neurons and anchored the spatial code in RSC.
evidence: Supported by two-photon imaging data and population vector analysis

claim: Landmark encoding in RSC was more robust after task acquisition.
source: This encoding was more robust after task acquisition.
evidence: Supported by comparison of neural activity in naive vs expert animals

claim: Decoupling the virtual environment from mouse behavior degraded spatial representations in RSC.
source: Decoupling the virtual environment from mouse behavior degraded spatial representations and provided evidence that supralinear integration of visual and motor inputs contributes to landmark encoding.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing active navigation to decoupled stimulus presentation

claim: Supralinear integration of visual and motor inputs contributes to landmark encoding in RSC.
source: Decoupling the virtual environment from mouse behavior degraded spatial representations and provided evidence that supralinear integration of visual and motor inputs contributes to landmark encoding.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing that linear sum of visual and motor inputs is less than observed responses during active navigation

claim: V1 axons recorded in RSC were less modulated by task engagement than RSC neurons.
source: V1 axons recorded in RSC were less modulated by task engagement but showed surprisingly similar spatial tuning.
evidence: Supported by comparison of V1 bouton responses during virtual navigation vs decoupled stimulus presentation

claim: V1 axons recorded in RSC showed similar spatial tuning to RSC neurons.
source: V1 axons recorded in RSC were less modulated by task engagement but showed surprisingly similar spatial tuning.
evidence: Supported by imaging data of V1 axonal boutons in RSC during task execution

claim: Landmark representations in RSC are the result of local integration of visual, motor, and spatial information.
source: Our data indicate that landmark representations in RSC are the result of local integration of visual, motor, and spatial information.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing supralinear integration and comparison of V1 inputs to RSC outputs

claim: Visual landmarks are advantageous for efficient navigation as information-rich reference points for self-location and route planning.
source: Visual landmarks are particularly advantageous for efficient navigation, representing information-rich reference points for self-location and route planning (Etienne et al., 1996; Gothard et al., 1996b; Jeffery, 1998; Knierim et al., 1995; McNaughton et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on landmark-based navigation

claim: Distal landmarks can provide critical orientation cues to find goal locations even when immediate surroundings are not informative.
source: Even in situations where the immediate surroundings may not be informative, distal landmarks can provide critical orientation cues to find goal locations (Morris, 1981; Tolman, 1948).
evidence: Supported by citations to classic studies on spatial navigation

claim: Salient visuo-spatial cues anchor almost every type of spatially-tuned cells observed in the mammalian brain.
source: Their importance is further underlined by the fact that salient visuo-spatial cues anchor almost every type of spatially-tuned cells observed in the mammalian brain to date, including head-direction cells (Jacob et al., 2017; Taube et al., 1990; Yoder et al., 2011), hippocampal place cells (Buzsáki, 2005; Jeffery, 1998), and grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (Hafting et al., 2005; Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on head-direction cells, place cells, and grid cells

claim: Landmarks exert powerful influence on the head-direction system even when self-motion feedback conflicts with external visual cues.
source: Even in scenarios where self-motion feedback is in conflict with external visual cues, landmarks exert powerful influence on the head-direction system (Etienne and Jeffery, 2004; Valerio and Taube, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on head-direction system and landmark influence

claim: Theoretical studies have shown the importance of landmarks for error correction during spatial computations.
source: A number of theoretical studies have shown the importance of landmarks for error correction during spatial computations (Burgess et al., 2007; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Monaco et al., 2011; Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical modeling studies

claim: It remains poorly understood how visual information is integrated into spatial code for goal-directed behavior.
source: However, it remains poorly understood how visual information is integrated into spatial code for goal-directed behavior.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field

claim: Studies in humans with damage to RSC suggest a key role for RSC in utilizing familiar visual cues for navigation.
source: Studies in humans with damage to RSC, as well as functional imaging studies, suggest a key role for RSC in utilizing familiar visual cues for navigation (Auger et al., 2012; Epstein, 2008; Epstein and Vass, 2014; Maguire, 2001; Vann et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to human lesion and imaging studies

claim: RSC exhibits some of the earliest measurable metabolic dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Additionally, RSC exhibits some of the earliest measurable metabolic dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Minoshima et al., 1997; Pengas et al., 2010; Villain et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on metabolic dysfunction in AD

claim: RSC plays a role in general mnemonic processing.
source: This is consistent with the putative roles of RSC in general mnemonic processing (Cooper et al., 2001; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006; Valenstein et al., 1987) and route-planning (Spiers and Maguire, 2006), both of which are hallmarks of cognitive decline in AD patients (Vann et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on RSC function in memory

claim: RSC plays a role in route-planning.
source: This is consistent with the putative roles of RSC in general mnemonic processing (Cooper et al., 2001; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006; Valenstein et al., 1987) and route-planning (Spiers and Maguire, 2006), both of which are hallmarks of cognitive decline in AD patients (Vann et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on route-planning

claim: Lesion studies in rodents indicate that RSC is important for navigating based on self-motion cues alone.
source: Lesion studies in rodents indicate that RSC is also important for navigating based on self-motion cues alone (Elduayen and Save, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to rodent lesion study

claim: RSC is situated at the intersection of areas that encode visual information, motor feedback, higher-order decision making, and the hippocampal formation.
source: These findings are congruent with known RSC anatomy: situated at the intersection of areas that encode visual information, motor feedback, higher-order decision making, and the hippocampal formation (van Groen and Wyss, 1992; Kononenko and Witter, 2012; Miyashita and Rockland, 2007; Sugar et al., 2011), RSC is ideally positioned to integrate these inputs to guide ongoing behavior.
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies of RSC connectivity

claim: RSC is ideally positioned to integrate visual, motor, decision-making, and hippocampal inputs to guide ongoing behavior.
source: These findings are congruent with known RSC anatomy: situated at the intersection of areas that encode visual information, motor feedback, higher-order decision making, and the hippocampal formation (van Groen and Wyss, 1992; Kononenko and Witter, 2012; Miyashita and Rockland, 2007; Sugar et al., 2011), RSC is ideally positioned to integrate these inputs to guide ongoing behavior.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical connectivity and functional roles

claim: Individual RSC neurons conjunctively encode space in egocentric and allocentric spatial reference frames.
source: Electrophysiological recordings in freely moving rats have shown that individual RSC neurons conjunctively encode space in egocentric and allocentric spatial reference frames (Alexander and Nitz, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to electrophysiology study in rats

claim: RSC neurons exhibit single, spatially tuned receptive fields in one-dimensional environments.
source: When placed in a one-dimensional environment, RSC neurons exhibit single, spatially tuned receptive fields (Mao et al., 2017), while in two-dimensional environments (Alexander and Nitz, 2017) they were found to express multiple receptive fields.
evidence: Supported by citation to study on RSC spatial tuning

claim: RSC neurons express multiple receptive fields in two-dimensional environments.
source: When placed in a one-dimensional environment, RSC neurons exhibit single, spatially tuned receptive fields (Mao et al., 2017), while in two-dimensional environments (Alexander and Nitz, 2017) they were found to express multiple receptive fields.
evidence: Supported by citation to study on RSC spatial tuning in 2D environments

claim: RSC neurons encode context as well as task-related cues such as goal location.
source: RSC neurons have further been shown to encode context as well as task-related cues such as goal location (Smith et al., 2012; Vedder et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on RSC encoding of context and goals

claim: A subset of cells in RSC encode head-direction in a way that is particularly sensitive to local environmental cues.
source: Finally, a subset of cells in RSC also encode head-direction in a way that is particularly sensitive to local environmental cues (Jacob et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on head-direction cells in RSC

claim: Visual inputs are important for RSC function.
source: A common theme across these studies is the importance of visual inputs for RSC function.
evidence: Inference from multiple cited studies on RSC

claim: Visual cues alone are sufficient to guide behavior.
source: While the role of proximal, non-visual cues, such as whisker stimulation, has not been thoroughly evaluated, it is clear that visual cues alone are sufficient to guide behavior (Etienne et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on visual guidance of behavior

claim: Mice learned to use visual cues to locate reward zones along the corridor.
source: Mice learned to use the visual cues to locate the reward zones along the corridor (Figure 1C, mean 32.3 ± 3.6 training sessions for n = 10 mice).
evidence: Supported by behavioral training data showing learning over sessions

claim: Mice required an average of 32.3 ± 3.6 training sessions to learn the task.
source: Mice learned to use the visual cues to locate the reward zones along the corridor (Figure 1C, mean 32.3 ± 3.6 training sessions for n = 10 mice).
evidence: Quantitative data from behavioral training

claim: Licking behavior of expert animals was significantly spatially modulated.
source: Licking behavior of expert animals was significantly spatially modulated (mean ± SEM: 13.48 ± 1.23, n = 12 session, 11 mice), making it an accurate behavioral assay.
evidence: Supported by spatial modulation z-score analysis of licking behavior

claim: Task scores on trials with optogenetic stimulation were significantly lower compared to trials with only masking light.
source: Task scores on trials with stimulation was significantly lower compared to trials where only the masking light was shown within the same session (43.7 ± 7.4 cm vs. 24.3 ± 6.2 cm, n = 5 mice, paired t-test: p = 0.003, Figure 1F), indicating that RSC activity contributes to successful execution of this behavior.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic inactivation experiment data

claim: RSC activity contributes to successful execution of the landmark navigation task.
source: Task scores on trials with stimulation was significantly lower compared to trials where only the masking light was shown within the same session (43.7 ± 7.4 cm vs. 24.3 ± 6.2 cm, n = 5 mice, paired t-test: p = 0.003, Figure 1F), indicating that RSC activity contributes to successful execution of this behavior.
evidence: Inference from optogenetic inactivation results showing behavioral deficit

claim: On average, 120.0 ± 17.56 RSC neurons were recorded per mouse.
source: On average, we recorded 120.0 ± 17.56 RSC neurons per mouse (n = 7 mice).
evidence: Quantitative data from two-photon imaging experiments

claim: The majority of RSC neurons found to be task engaged were aligned to the visual landmark.
source: The majority of RSC neurons found to be task engaged were aligned to the visual landmark (Figure 2C, n = 55 short trial onset and 62 long trial onset, 206 and 235 landmark, 101 and 118 reward neurons, respectively; seven mice; mean ± SEM fractions of aligned neurons: trial onset: 5.6 ± 0.3%, landmark: 22.3 ± 1.6%, reward: 11.6 ± 0.7%; one way ANOVAshort: p = 0.0023; ANOVAlong: p<0.001, Tukey's HSD post-hoc pairwise comparison with Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by classification of neurons based on alignment to task features

claim: A smaller but sizeable fraction of RSC neurons were aligned to the reward point.
source: A smaller but sizeable fraction of RSC neurons were aligned to the reward point, suggesting that RSC also encodes behavioral goals as well, and the onset of a trial, regardless of where an animal was placed on the track relative to the visual landmark.
evidence: Supported by neuron classification data showing reward-aligned neurons

claim: RSC encodes behavioral goals.
source: A smaller but sizeable fraction of RSC neurons were aligned to the reward point, suggesting that RSC also encodes behavioral goals as well, and the onset of a trial, regardless of where an animal was placed on the track relative to the visual landmark.
evidence: Inference from presence of reward-aligned neurons

claim: Egocentric (trial onset) as well as allocentric (landmark and reward) variables are encoded in RSC during landmark-based navigation.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Alexander and Nitz, 2015), these data indicate that egocentric (trial onset) as well as allocentric (landmark and reward) variables are encoded in RSC during landmark-based navigation.
evidence: Supported by neuron classification data and comparison to previous literature

claim: The vast majority of neurons showed a single peak of activity in the task.
source: The vast majority of neurons showed a single peak of activity in our task.
evidence: Observation from analysis of neuronal activity patterns

claim: Landmark neurons provided significantly higher trial type decoding accuracy compared to trial onset or reward-aligned neurons.
source: While trial onset or reward-aligned neurons provided only chance level decoding or slightly better (trial onset: median 53.44% correct; reward: 62.1%), trial type decoding by landmark neurons was significantly higher (82.56%, Kruskal-Wallis test p=0.015; post-hoc Mann-Whitney U pairwise testing with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Supported by template matching decoder analysis

claim: Layer 5 contained substantially fewer landmark neurons than layer 2/3.
source: However, L5 contained substantially fewer landmark neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C; One-way ANOVA, p<10–8, Tukey HSD post-hoc test with Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by laminar analysis of neuron types

claim: Only a small number of neurons were found to be tuned to landmark identity.
source: Only a small number of neurons were found to be tuned to landmark identity (Figure 2H), with most neurons showing no specific preference.
evidence: Supported by landmark selectivity index analysis

claim: Neurons in RSC encode a mix of task variables with a strong preference for visual cues informing the animal about goal locations.
source: These results indicate that neurons in RSC encode a mix of task variables with a strong preference for visual cues informing the animal about goal locations.
evidence: Inference from neuron classification and selectivity analyses

claim: The spatial code in RSC is sharpest at the landmark.
source: Slices of the cross-correlation matrix (Figure 3C and F, taken at the dashed lines indicated in 3B and 3E), reveal that the spatial code is sharpest at the landmark.
evidence: Supported by population vector cross-correlation analysis shown in figures

claim: The cross-correlation at the animal's true location significantly increases as the animal approaches the landmark and remains elevated until it reaches the reward.
source: The cross-correlation at the animal's true location (i.e. along the diagonal from top left to bottom right) significantly increases as the animal approaches the landmark and remains elevated until it reaches the reward (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by population vector cross-correlation analysis

claim: Location reconstruction error was significantly lower when neural activity was aligned to landmarks rather than trial onset.
source: We observed a significantly lower location reconstruction error when neural activity was aligned to landmarks, rather than trial onset (Figure 3H, mean ± SEM: 3.7 ± 0.61 vs. 5.27 ± 0.56 short trials; 3.23 ± 0.48 vs. 5.26 ± 0.42, unpaired, 2-tailed t-test: p<0.016 (short), p<0.001 (long)).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of population vector cross-correlation

claim: There was no significant difference in reconstruction error between short track and long track trials.
source: Finally, we found no significant difference in reconstruction error between short track and long track trials, as most neurons are active on both trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of reconstruction errors across trial types

claim: RSC has a spatial code that is strongly modulated by environmental cues to inform the animal about the location of its goal.
source: These results provide evidence for a spatial code in RSC that is strongly modulated by environmental cues to inform the animal about the location of its goal.
evidence: Inference from population vector analysis showing landmark anchoring

claim: There was a significant decrease in neuronal responses during decoupled stimulus presentation compared to virtual navigation.
source: We found a significant decrease in neuronal responses in this condition (Figure 4B and C, mean ± SEM VR: 0.17 ± 0.005, mean decoupled: 0.059 ± 0.004, paired, two-tailed t-test: p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by comparison of neural responses during active navigation vs passive viewing

claim: Activity in RSC is strongly dependent on active task engagement.
source: This result suggests that activity in RSC is strongly dependent on active task engagement.
evidence: Inference from decreased responses during decoupled stimulus presentation

claim: Population activity showed significantly less spatial specificity during decoupled stimulus presentation.
source: Congruent with this, population activity showed significantly less spatial specificity during decoupled stimulus presentation (Figure 4E–H, mean reconstruction error ± SEM: 3.7 ± 0.61 vs. 7.88 ± 0.78 short trials; 3.23 ± 0.48 vs. 11.16 ± 1.18, unpaired, Mann-Whitney U: p<0.001 (short), p<0.001 (long)).
evidence: Supported by population vector cross-correlation analysis during decoupled presentation

claim: Encoding of behaviorally-relevant variables in RSC is modulated by ongoing behavior, rather than being driven solely by sensory inputs.
source: This indicates that encoding of behaviorally-relevant variables in RSC is modulated by ongoing behavior, rather than being driven solely by sensory inputs.
evidence: Inference from comparison of active navigation vs decoupled stimulus presentation

claim: The standard error of the distance of individual transients to the peak of the mean trace was lower during virtual navigation compared to decoupled stimulus presentation.
source: We found that the standard error of the distance of individual transients to the peak of the mean trace (Figure 4J, median jitter (cm): shortVR = 4.67, shortDC = 8.66; longVR = 5.75, longDC = 9.85) was lower during virtual navigation compared to decoupled stimulus presentation.
evidence: Supported by analysis of transient spatial jitter

claim: There was a significant reduction in the number of transients per trial during decoupled stimulus presentation.
source: Furthermore, we saw a significant reduction in the number of transients per trial during decoupled stimulus presentation (Figure 4K, median values (transients/trial): shortVR = 0.45, shortDC = 0.14; longVR = 0.45, longDC = 0.14), but only very little change in the amplitude of individual transients (Figure 4L, median values (∆F/F): shortVR = 1.48, shortDC = 1.36; longVR = 1.4, longDC = 1.33, Kruskal-Wallis test p<0.001; Mann-Whitney-U pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction results indicated, ***=p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of transient properties

claim: Changes during decoupled stimulus presentation are due to poorer spatial anchoring of activity and fewer instances of a given neuron exhibiting a transient.
source: These results show that the changes during decoupled stimulus presentation is due to poorer spatial anchoring of activity and fewer instances of a given neuron to exhibit a transient.
evidence: Inference from analysis of transient jitter and frequency

claim: When landmark presentation occurred during locomotion, activity was significantly increased compared to passive viewing.
source: When landmark presentation occurred during locomotion, activity was significantly increased (Figure 5C, n = 127 neurons, five mice, mean ± SEM number of trials/neuron: 13.0 ± 0.41 resting, 9.3 ± 0.3 running; peak mean ∆F/F ± SEM: VR: 0.93 ± 0.06, landmark + motor: 0.57 ± 0.06, landmark, no motor: 0.22 ± 0.04, Kruskal-Wallis test: p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U post-hoc comparison with Bonferroni correction: p<0.001 for all shown comparisons).
evidence: Supported by comparison of neural responses during locomotion vs rest during decoupled presentation

claim: Visual inputs alone or visual inputs plus locomotion did not elicit the same response as virtual navigation.
source: However, we found that visual inputs alone or visual inputs plus locomotion did not elicit the same response as virtual navigation (Figure 5C,D, Kruskal-Wallis test: p<0.001; post-hoc Mann-Whitney-U and Bonferroni correction: p<0.001 for all shown comparisons).
evidence: Supported by comparison of responses across different conditions

claim: The linear sum of 'motor only' and 'landmark, no motor' remained lower than the mean amplitude recorded during 'landmark + motor'.
source: Finally we asked whether the linear sum of 'motor only' and 'landmark, no motor' added up to 'landmark + motor' (Figure 5D and E). We found that the linear sum approached, but remained lower than the mean amplitude recorded during 'landmark + motor'.
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison of linear sum vs observed responses

claim: There is substantial nonlinear integration of visual and motor inputs in RSC neurons during goal-directed virtual navigation.
source: Together these results provide evidence for substantial nonlinear integration of visual and motor inputs in RSC neurons during goal-directed virtual navigation as well as decreased, but still significant, nonlinear processing during decoupled stimulus presentation.
evidence: Inference from comparison of linear sum vs observed responses

claim: Only a small number of neurons showed modulation of transient amplitude by running speed.
source: We found only a small number of neurons showing modulation of transient amplitude by running speed across the population of task-active neurons (Figure 4—figure supplements 1B, 0.5% on short trials n = 29 neurons and 15.6% on long trials n = 51 neurons).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of transient amplitude and running speed

claim: Some neurons that previously had not expressed discernible spatially tuned activity established spatial receptive fields after learning.
source: We found some neurons that previously had not expressed discernible spatially tuned activity, establishing spatial receptive fields, while showed amplified responses (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of neural activity in naive vs expert animals

claim: The encoding of space in the naïve animal was much degraded compared to expert animals.
source: When we identified task active neurons in expert animals and calculated the population vector cross correlation during naïve and expert sessions, we found that the encoding of space in the naïve animal was much degraded (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by population vector cross-correlation analysis in naive vs expert sessions

claim: Neurons in the naïve animal showed significantly worse representation of the animal's location compared to expert animals.
source: To test this, we identified task active neurons in naïve and expert sessions independently and calculated the population vector cross correlation. Neurons in the naïve animal showed significantly worse representation of the animal's location (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by independent analysis of task-active neurons in each session

claim: The observed neural activity in expert animals is the result of a code that develops in RSC as animals learn to associate the visual cue with a reward location.
source: The observed neural activity in expert animals is thus the result of a code that develops in RSC as animals learn to associate the visual cue with a reward location, turning it into a spatial landmark.
evidence: Inference from comparison of naive vs expert neural activity

claim: V1 axons exhibited comparable receptive field tunings as RSC neurons.
source: Using the same landmark-dependent navigation task, we found that V1 axons exhibited comparable receptive field tunings as RSC neurons.
evidence: Supported by imaging of V1 axonal boutons in RSC during task execution

claim: V1 axon responses were substantially less modulated by task engagement compared to RSC neurons.
source: However, these responses were substantially less modulated by task engagement (Figure 7I), suggesting that V1 axons encode visual features more faithfully.
evidence: Supported by comparison of V1 bouton vs RSC neuron responses during active vs decoupled conditions

claim: V1 axons encode visual features more faithfully than RSC neurons.
source: However, these responses were substantially less modulated by task engagement (Figure 7I), suggesting that V1 axons encode visual features more faithfully.
evidence: Inference from lesser modulation by task engagement

claim: At least a subpopulation of RSC-projecting neurons in V1 is tuned to behaviorally-relevant visual cues to a previously unknown extent.
source: The specificity of these responses suggests that at least a subpopulation of RSC-projecting neurons in V1 is tuned to behaviorally-relevant visual cues to a previously unknown extent.
evidence: Inference from observed spatial tuning of V1 boutons in RSC

claim: V1 inputs represent visual inputs more faithfully and are less modulated by context than RSC neurons themselves.
source: Despite their specificity, however, they represent visual inputs more faithfully and are less modulated by context than RSC neurons themselves, pointing to the local computations performed in RSC.
evidence: Inference from comparison of V1 bouton and RSC neuron responses

claim: The task required animals to discriminate visual cues, use them to localize themselves in space, and navigate to a rewarded zone based on self-motion feedback.
source: The task required animals to discriminate visual cues, use them to localize themselves in space, and navigate to a rewarded zone based on self-motion feedback.
evidence: Description of task design and requirements

claim: Landmarks anchored the majority of task-active neurons in dysgranular RSC.
source: Using this paradigm, we found that landmarks anchored the majority of task-active neurons in dysgranular RSC (Figure 2C and D) and significantly sharpened the representation of the animal's current location in the population code (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by neuron classification and population vector analysis

claim: Landmarks significantly sharpened the representation of the animal's current location in the population code.
source: Using this paradigm, we found that landmarks anchored the majority of task-active neurons in dysgranular RSC (Figure 2C and D) and significantly sharpened the representation of the animal's current location in the population code (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by population vector cross-correlation analysis

claim: The spatial representation in RSC largely changed during learning.
source: This spatial representation largely changed 2during learning (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by comparison of naive vs expert neural activity

claim: Landmark responses were not the result of simple visual and/or motor drive.
source: Landmark responses were not the result of simple visual and/or motor drive: showing the same visual stimuli while the animals were not engaged in the task elicited significantly attenuated responses (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by comparison of responses during active navigation vs decoupled presentation

claim: Coinciding visual input and motor feedback during decoupled stimulus presentation did not elicit the same response amplitudes as observed during active navigation.
source: Coinciding visual input and motor feedback during decoupled stimulus presentation did not elicit the same response amplitudes as observed during active navigation (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by comparison of responses across different conditions

claim: Receptive fields expressed by V1 axonal boutons were strikingly similar to those recorded from RSC neurons.
source: Interestingly, receptive fields expressed by V1 axonal boutons in animals executing the same behavior were strikingly similar to those recorded from RSC neurons (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by imaging of V1 boutons during task execution

claim: V1 boutons were less modulated by active task engagement than RSC neurons, indicating a hierarchy of sequential processing.
source: However, they were less modulated by active task engagement (Figure 7H and I), indicating a hierarchy of sequential processing.
evidence: Inference from comparison of modulation by task engagement

claim: The task combines visual landmark use for self-localization with path integration to successfully find rewards.
source: We describe a task that combines both of these navigational strategies: animals are required to use visual landmarks for self-localization, followed by path integration to successfully find rewards.
evidence: Description of task design combining multiple navigation strategies

claim: There was a deficit in the animal's ability to use landmarks to guide localizing rewards during RSC inactivation.
source: Using optogenetic inactivation on a randomized subset of trials we found a deficit in the animal's ability to use landmarks to guide localizing rewards (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic inactivation experiment results

claim: Spatial representations in RSC are anchored by allocentric (landmark) cues and maintained by self-motion feedback after the animal has passed the visual cue.
source: In contrast, we find that spatial representations in RSC are anchored by allocentric (landmark) cues and maintained by self-motion feedback after the animal has passed the visual cue (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by population vector analysis showing landmark anchoring and sustained activity

claim: Simple linear summation of visual and motor inputs was insufficient to explain landmark encoding in RSC.
source: We found that simple linear summation of visual and motor inputs was insufficient to explain landmark encoding in RSC.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing linear sum is less than observed responses

claim: A nonlinear mechanism (or multiple mechanisms) underlie the integration of visual and motor variables to produce robust visuo-spatial responses during navigation.
source: Instead, a nonlinear mechanism (or multiple mechanisms) underlie the integration of these variables to produce robust visuo-spatial responses during navigation.
evidence: Inference from failure of linear summation to explain responses

claim: Active navigation (in virtual reality) sharpened spatial tuning and increased robustness of encoding in RSC compared to viewing the movie without being engaged in the task.
source: Active navigation (in virtual reality) sharpened spatial tuning and increased robustness of encoding in RSC compared to viewing the movie without being engaged in the task.
evidence: Supported by comparison of spatial tuning and transient properties across conditions

claim: The amplitude of recorded transients was unchanged between active navigation and decoupled presentation, suggesting the presence of a thresholding process in the circuit.
source: Interestingly, the amplitude of recorded transients was unchanged, suggesting the presence of a thresholding process in the circuit (Figure 4I–L).
evidence: Inference from observation that transient amplitude is similar across conditions

claim: Locomotion during decoupled stimulus presentation significantly increased the robustness of encoding while having very little effect on the fidelity of spatial tuning or transient amplitude.
source: Locomotion during decoupled stimulus presentation significantly increased the robustness of encoding while having very little effect on the fidelity of spatial tuning or transient amplitude.
evidence: Supported by analysis of transient properties during locomotion vs rest

claim: Motor input broadly pushes neurons towards spiking but does not contribute to spatial tuning.
source: This indicates that motor input broadly pushes neurons towards spiking but does not contribute to its spatial tuning (Figure 5F–I).
evidence: Inference from analysis showing increased transient frequency but not improved spatial tuning with locomotion

claim: Visual input alone is insufficient to explain the fidelity of spatial tuning observed during virtual navigation.
source: Furthermore, our data show that visual input alone is insufficient to explain the fidelity of spatial tuning we observed during virtual navigation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of responses to visual input alone vs during active navigation

claim: The most likely mechanism underlying supralinear integration in RSC is the multiplicative effects of significantly improved fidelity of spatial tuning and increased likelihood of emitting transients within a neurons receptive field.
source: Our results indicate that the most likely mechanism underlying supralinear integration in RSC is the multiplicative effects of significantly improved fidelity of spatial tuning and increased likelihood of emitting transients within a neurons receptive field.
evidence: Inference from analysis of spatial tuning and transient properties

claim: Animals developed a more robust code for space during task acquisition.
source: Animals developed a more robust code for space during task acquisition (Figure 6E and F), suggesting that this supralinear mechanism may be the result of learning the spatial significance of a visual landmark cue.
evidence: Supported by comparison of spatial coding in naive vs expert animals

claim: The supralinear integration mechanism may be the result of learning the spatial significance of a visual landmark cue.
source: Animals developed a more robust code for space during task acquisition (Figure 6E and F), suggesting that this supralinear mechanism may be the result of learning the spatial significance of a visual landmark cue.
evidence: Speculation based on observation of learning-related changes

claim: The spatial tuning observed in task active neurons in dysgranular RSC appears similar to those of place cells.
source: The spatial tuning we observed in task active neurons in dysgranular RSC appears similar to those of place cells (see Figure 2B and Figure 3A and D).
evidence: Comparison to known properties of place cells

claim: RSC is strongly biased to encode behaviorally relevant visual cues that inform the animal about the location of a reward.
source: However, RSC may not exhibit spatial representations that differ from CA1 when sensory information regarding goals is absent. Consistent with this, we find that RSC is strongly biased to encode behaviorally relevant visual cues that inform the animal about the location of a reward.
evidence: Inference from observation that most neurons are landmark-aligned

claim: A robust spatial code in RSC only emerges after learning the spatial significance of the visual cues.
source: This robust code only emerges after learning the spatial significance of the visual cues (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by comparison of naive vs expert neural activity

claim: RSC's bias to encode behaviorally relevant stimuli is particularly interesting in light of its relationship with axonal inputs from V1.
source: RSC's bias to encode behaviorally relevant stimuli is particularly interesting in light of its relationship with axonal inputs from V1 (Figure 7).
evidence: Inference connecting RSC encoding properties to V1 inputs

claim: V1 axons exhibited comparable receptive field tunings as RSC neurons but were substantially less modulated by task engagement, suggesting that V1 axons encode visual features more faithfully.
source: Using the same landmark-dependent navigation task, we found that V1 axons exhibited comparable receptive field tunings as RSC neurons. However, these responses were substantially less modulated by task engagement (Figure 7I), suggesting that V1 axons encode visual features more faithfully.
evidence: Supported by comparison of V1 bouton and RSC neuron responses

claim: The modulation observed in V1 may be the result of strong top-down inputs from RSC itself or from other regions.
source: The modulation we did observe may be the result of strong top-down inputs from RSC itself (Makino and Komiyama, 2015) or from other regions (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation based on known anatomical connections and citations

claim: Activity in RSC is more correlated with V1 during locomotion compared to quiescent periods.
source: This is congruent with a recent study showing that activity in RSC is more correlated with V1 during locomotion compared to quiescent periods (Clancy et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study

claim: Before learning the behavioral significance of visual features in a novel environment, RSC may initially receive purely visual inputs from V1.
source: Indeed, before learning the behavioral significance of visual features in a novel environment, RSC may initially receive purely visual inputs from V1.
evidence: Speculation about learning-related changes in V1-RSC interactions

claim: As the animal learns to navigate in a new environment, feedback from RSC to V1 may lead to modulated responses based on behavioral relevance in primary visual cortex.
source: As the animal learns to navigate in the new environment, feedback from RSC to V1 (as well as other areas such as ACC) may lead to modulated responses based on behavioral relevance in primary visual cortex, as reported by an increasing number of studies (Attinger et al., 2017; Pakan et al., 2018; Poort et al., 2015; Saleem et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to studies showing behavioral modulation in V1

claim: RSC may act as a critical processing node that gates behaviorally relevant visual inputs and relays them to the entorhinal cortex and other areas involved in spatial navigation.
source: Our data provide evidence that RSC may act as a critical processing node that gates behaviorally relevant visual inputs and relays them to the entorhinal cortex and other areas involved in spatial navigation, where its readout may be used to anchor spatially tuned neurons such as grid cells (Burak and Fiete, 2009; Campbell et al., 2018) or head-direction cells (Jacob et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation about RSC's role in broader navigation circuits, supported by citations

claim: Functional imaging studies show RSC to be uniquely engaged during landmark-based navigation.
source: While RSC receives inputs from V2, M2, and other cortical areas (Oh et al., 2014; Sugar et al., 2011), functional imaging studies show RSC to be uniquely engaged during landmark-based navigation (Auger et al., 2012; Epstein, 2008; Epstein and Vass, 2014; Maguire, 2001; Vann et al., 2009), suggesting RSC is indeed a key locus for integrating visual and spatial information compared to other association areas.
evidence: Supported by citations to functional imaging studies

claim: RSC is a key locus for integrating visual and spatial information compared to other association areas.
source: While RSC receives inputs from V2, M2, and other cortical areas (Oh et al., 2014; Sugar et al., 2011), functional imaging studies show RSC to be uniquely engaged during landmark-based navigation (Auger et al., 2012; Epstein, 2008; Epstein and Vass, 2014; Maguire, 2001; Vann et al., 2009), suggesting RSC is indeed a key locus for integrating visual and spatial information compared to other association areas.
evidence: Inference from functional imaging data showing unique engagement of RSC

claim: The results are consistent with data from humans with RSC lesions who show an impaired ability to use environmental cues for navigation.
source: Finally, this work provides novel insights into the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive computations. Our results are consistent with data from humans with RSC lesions who show an impaired ability to use environmental cues for navigation, as well as neuroimaging studies that show increased activity in RSC during spatial behaviors (Cho and Sharp, 2001; Ino et al., 2007; Julian et al., 2018; Maguire, 2001; Robertson et al., 2016; Vann et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison to human lesion and imaging studies

claim: Neuroimaging studies show increased activity in RSC during spatial behaviors.
source: Finally, this work provides novel insights into the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive computations. Our results are consistent with data from humans with RSC lesions who show an impaired ability to use environmental cues for navigation, as well as neuroimaging studies that show increased activity in RSC during spatial behaviors (Cho and Sharp, 2001; Ino et al., 2007; Julian et al., 2018; Maguire, 2001; Robertson et al., 2016; Vann et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuroimaging studies

claim: Leveraging RSC to unravel how multiple input streams are integrated during higher level associative processes like navigation may provide novel insights into the mechanisms of cognition and its dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease and other brain disorders.
source: Leveraging RSC to unravel how multiple input streams are integrated during higher level associative processes like navigation may in the future provide novel insights into the mechanisms of cognition and its dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease and other currently intractable brain disorders.
evidence: Speculation about future implications of understanding RSC function
